summary:
Iraq's legal position for a trans visitor is set by the amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution passed by the Council of Representatives on 27 April 2024, signed by the President on 29 June 2024 and in force since 1 July 2024. The amendment criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. Human Rights Watch, the Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor and ILGA Asia all record it as the operative legal baseline, and Human Rights Watch has called for its repeal.

Penalties are custodial and severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, applied to the trans person and to the doctor, which places transition itself outside the law. The legislation also penalises "promoting homosexuality". Penalties include fines and deportation, so removal from the country is a stated consequence of a criminalised status rather than a discretionary immigration outcome.

Iraq has no legal gender recognition framework. The 2024 provisions target "biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination" with up to three years' imprisonment for the person and the practitioner, excluding court-ordered procedures on intersex people. No route to corrected identity documents exists, and a visitor cannot rely on Iraqi documents matching their presentation.

Partner recognition is closed. The Personal Status Law 1959 Article 3 and the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 Article 1 define marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are illegal. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognised status, and the relationship itself falls within the 2024 criminalisation.

Violence against LGBT Iraqis is documented over more than a decade with no effective state response. A BBC investigation found that killings of gay people had continued over successive years while the authorities turned a blind eye, and reported the UN's assessment that state neglect makes the state itself a perpetrator. In October 2023 a prominent Iraqi social media figure was fatally shot in Baghdad during a crackdown on the LGBT community. In early 2012 Shi'a militia death squads carried out the "Emo Killings", targeting teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing; flyers appeared in Baghdad naming individuals and threatening them unless they cut their hair and abandoned nonconformist dress. The pattern is one of impunity for anti-LGBT violence rather than prosecution of it.

Official assessments acknowledge the danger. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Iraq recorded societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity, alongside sectarian violence, torture and impunity. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 3.0, July 2025) assesses risk from state, hybrid and non-state actors, the availability of protection, the feasibility of internal relocation, and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 amendment was passed by the Council of Representatives after a period in which the climate for LGBT Iraqis hardened; supporters framed the measure as upholding religious values, and rights organisations condemned it and called for repeal.

Marriage formalities differ by instrument. Article 7 of the Personal Status Law 1959 requires couples seeking to marry to produce medical documents proving they are not infected with AIDS, and a 1981 amendment to the same law allows a wife to divorce a husband guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity.

Marriage law is not uniform across the country: the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 mirrors the federal Personal Status Law 1959 in defining marriage as a union between a man and a woman, so neither the federal framework nor the Kurdistan Region framework recognises a same-sex marriage or civil union.
localsOnly:
Support and relocation work is carried largely by non-governmental organisations. Iraqi LGBT, established in September 2005, relocates LGBTQ people to safer countries, provides legal help to asylum seekers and maintains safe houses inside Iraq. The International Railroad for Queer Refugees, founded in 2008, provides financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing prosecution for sexual orientation or gender identity.

OWFI led more than 40 local organisations in changing Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had allowed only government-run shelters to operate. Rasan has run larger projects since 2016 as a partner of COC Nederland under the Pride Program, locally named Crossing Iraqi Rainbow. Iraqueer, formed in March 2015, runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, YouTube videos and workshops on gender and sexuality, and advocacy on safety in crisis.
outOfScopeNotes:
The number of prosecutions brought under the 2024 amendment is not sourced; the statute's text and its entry into force are documented, but enforcement data are not available in the material reviewed.

Historical material on the 1986 order relocating Iraqis with AIDS to a prison facility is not trans-specific and is not treated as evidence of the current legal regime.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note is an asylum-decision instrument rather than a travel advisory; its risk assessment is used here for its country information on state, hybrid and non-state actors and internal relocation.

The US State Department report dates from 2012 and predates the 2024 statute; it documents the pre-statutory climate and official acknowledgment of discrimination and violence.
